key_points: Large-bore chest tubes are generally defined as ≥20 F; inner diameter varies by material/manufacturer.
Clinical indications persist for high-PEEP ventilated pneumothorax, BPF, emergencies/trauma, select hemothorax, and postthoracic surgery pneumothorax.
Surgical/blunt dissection via the mid-axillary 'safe triangle' is the preferred technique; trocar insertion is discouraged.
Three-bottle drainage systems (trap, water seal, manometer) underpin modern commercial drains; dry suction variants exist.
Small-bore tubes (<20 F) are often as effective as large-bore but with lower pain scores; choose size based on scenario rather than dogma.

clinical_procedures.name: Large-bore chest tube insertion – surgical/blunt dissection
steps: Position patient supine or ~45° with ipsilateral arm abducted and externally rotated.
Identify the safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, and a line superior to the nipple/submammary fold.
Prep and drape; infiltrate ~20 m L lidocaine to dermis, subcutaneous tissues, intercostal space/periosteum, and parietal pleura.
Aspirate air or fluid during anesthetic to confirm pleural entry; if none, reconfirm with ultrasound.
Make ~2 cm incision over the rib; bluntly dissect through serratus/intercostal muscles along the superior rib border.
Enter pleural space with closed instrument; open while withdrawing to avoid injury and allow egress of air/fluid.
Perform circumferential digital palpation to verify entry and assess adhesions.
Advance tube with Kelly clamp to guide direction (anterior–cranial for air; posterior–caudal for fluid); minimize spillage by proximal clamp as needed.
If significant resistance or kinking is encountered, suspect a false tract and correct before proceeding.
Secure with strong fixation suture (e.g., silk), anchor stitch, and connect to drainage system (typically −20 cm H2O suction for fluid; water seal for pneumothorax unless air evacuation inadequate).
notes: Avoid trocar insertion due to risk of penetrating trauma.

clinical_procedures.name: Seldinger technique for large-bore tubes (less common)
steps: Over-the-wire placement with serial dilation (up to three dilators may be required for catheters up to 32 F).
Lacks digital palpation and manual guidance advantages of the blunt dissection technique.
notes: Some manufacturers provide large-bore catheters for Seldinger placement.

clinical_procedures.name: Postprocedure management and removal
steps: Select analgesia with NSAIDs and/or opioids; NSAIDs do not impair pleurodesis at 3 months in malignant effusion.
Consider clamping trials for pneumothorax, noting ACCP expert split; digital air-leak devices can hasten removal if no leak is measured.
Outpatient Heimlich valve is reasonable for persistent air leak on water seal when criteria are met (asymptomatic, no subcutaneous emphysema after 14 days, stable pleural space).
For pleural effusion, reported removal thresholds vary widely (<100 to <500 m L/24 h); after lung resection, <5 m L/kg/24 h vs <200 m L/24 h show similar outcomes.
Remove the tube rapidly during positive intrathoracic pressure (patient humming) or during an inspiratory hold on the ventilator.

treatment_algorithms.title: Large bore chest tube surgical/blunt dissection technique algorithm
treatment_algorithms.condition: Chest tube insertion for pneumothorax or pleural fluid drainage
specific_recommendations: Attach the tube to a pleural drainage system—generally -20 cm H2O for fluid to water seal for pneumothoraces (unless unable to keep up with the evacuation of air).
decision_points_and_pathways: The “Safe Triangle” is the preferred location.
Guiding the tube anterior cranially for pneumothorax or posterior caudally for fluid is the general approach.
If no fluid nor air can be aspirated, reconfirming position with ultrasound can be invaluable.
Very little resistance should be felt, upon insertion. If significant resistance is felt or kinking is visualized—then tube has demonstrated a false path outside the chest wall cavity.
contraindications_and_exceptions: There are no absolute contraindications to chest tube placement in the setting of an emergency.
Relative contraindications include coagulopathies, pleural adhesions, loculated effusions, high riding diaphragms, or trauma with displacement of intraabdominal organs into the thoracic cavity.
monitoring_requirements: Verify proper tube position with a chest x-ray (also acceptable at the conclusion of the procedure).
The patency of the tube can be assessed by visualizing fluctuation of the fluid in the collection container.
alternative_approaches: Seldinger technique; some companies do provide large bore chest tubes that can be placed by this method.
Trocar method (otherwise known as the “harpoon”) which is discouraged.
treatment_algorithms.source_excerpt: Attach the tube to a pleural drainage system—generally -20 cm H2O for ﬂuid to water seal for pneumothoraces (unless unable to keep up with the evacuation of air).

clinical_applications.content: Use large-bore chest tubes (≥20 F) selectively: high-PEEP ventilated pneumothorax, anticipated BPF, traumatic chest injuries/hemothorax, and postthoracotomy pneumothorax.

practice_recommendations.content: Prefer blunt dissection in the triangle of safety; avoid trocar technique.
Direct tube anterior–cranial for pneumothorax and posterior–caudal for fluid; verify position radiographically.
Connect to appropriate drainage system (often −20 cm H2O suction for fluid; water seal for pneumothorax unless evacuation inadequate).

future_directions: Broader adoption and validation of digital air-leak monitoring to standardize removal decisions.
Further comparative effectiveness research on tube size and patient-centered outcomes across indications.
controversies: Optimal suction vs water seal strategy for postoperative air leaks.
Tube size selection in traumatic hemothorax and empyema; role of small-bore with adjuncts.

problems_observed.finding: Guidelines trend toward initial small-bore chest tubes, yet operators may still choose large-bore tubes initially.
problems_observed.details: The chapter states that while guidelines may support an initial small-bore approach, clinicians may elect to place a large-bore catheter first for reasons such as larger size, reduced kinking, or preference for a surgical approach.
problems_observed.reference: Chapter narrative, Indications/Contraindications; historical recommendation noted for pneumothorax sizing [5].

problems_observed.finding: Persistence of large-bore use despite evidence of no improved outcomes and increased pain.
problems_observed.details: Larger tube size has generally not resulted in better outcomes but has resulted in more pain; in the MIST1 trial registry, small-bore chest tubes (<20 F) were no less effective and had significantly lower pain scores than larger bore tubes.
problems_observed.reference: [2] Rahman et al., MIST1 trial registry.

guideline_adherence.implication: Align practice with evidence and guideline direction by using small-bore chest tubes as first-line in most cases to reduce pain without compromising efficacy, reserving large-bore tubes for clearly defined scenarios (e.g., traumatic injury/hemothorax, high-PEEP pneumothorax, bronchopleural fistula, emergencies, select post-thoracic surgery pneumothorax).

technology_and_technique.summary: Small-bore chest tubes (<20 F) were no less effective than large-bore (≥20 F) for pleural drainage, with significantly lower pain scores for small-bore devices. Larger tubes generally have not improved outcomes over the past 15–20 years.

technology_and_technique.topic: Technology enabling small-bore use in empyema
technology_and_technique.summary: Adoption of intrapleural lytics (t PA/DNase), ultrasound guidance, and catheter-flushing techniques has reduced the need for large-bore tubes in empyema without compromising outcomes.

technology_and_technique.topic: Patient selection for initial large-bore tube placement
technology_and_technique.summary: Consider large-bore chest tubes for: spontaneous pneumothorax on mechanical ventilation with high PEEP, bronchopleural fistula, emergencies, traumatic chest injuries, select hemothorax, and post-thoracic surgery pneumothorax. Many guidelines still support starting with small-bore when feasible.

technology_and_technique.topic: Guideline evolution for pneumothorax tube size
technology_and_technique.summary: Earlier recommendations (e.g., 2001 ACCP) suggested ~20 F for pneumothorax; contemporary practice trends toward smaller-bore tubes given comparable effectiveness and less pain.

Fanning (gas) and Hagen-Poiseuille (fluid) principles predict flow increases with radius to the 5th (gas) and 4th (fluid) power, respectively, favoring larger tubes theoretically; however, clinically, larger bore has not translated into better outcomes in most pleural infections/hemothorax scenarios.

Primary approach: surgical/blunt dissection. Less common: Seldinger and trocar methods. Large-bore tubes offer reduced kinking and a surgical approach advantage in select scenarios; no quantitative yield data provided.

Larger tubes are associated with more pain. Reported complications (no rates provided): malposition/misplacement, injury to surrounding structures, bleeding, subcutaneous emphysema, direct parenchymal injury, wound infection/empyema, re-expansion pulmonary edema, intercostal neuralgia.
technology_and_technique.reference: Chapter narrative; MIST 1 registry pain finding [2]

technology_and_technique.summary: Large-bore defined as ≥20 F. French scale measures outer diameter (mm = F × 0.333), e.g., 24 F ≈ 8 mm. Inner diameter varies by material/manufacturer and affects actual flow; consider when comparing devices.

points: Large-bore chest tubes (≥20 F) have narrower indications but remain important for specific scenarios such as ventilated pneumothorax with high PEEP, anticipated BPF, traumatic hemothorax, and select postoperative needs.
Blunt dissection through the triangle of safety with careful anatomy recognition reduces complications; trocar technique is discouraged.
Modern drainage systems derive from the three-bottle model; prioritize pain control and evidence-based removal strategies.
